We make the following assumptions throughout.

•

There is a probability triple (Ω,F,P) where

∘

P is the “true” or physical probability measure

∘

Ω is the universe of possible outcomes. We use ω∈Ω to represent a generic outcome, typically a sample path(s) of a stochastic process(es).

∘

the set F represents the set of possible events where an event is a subset of Ω.

•

There is also a filtration, {Ft​}t≥0​, that models the evolution of information through time. So for example, if it is known by time t whether or not an event, E, has occurred, then we have E∈Ft​. If we are working with a finite horizon, [0,T], then we can take F=FT​.

•

We also say that a stochastic process, Xt​, is Ft​-adapted if the value of Xt​ is known at time t when the information represented by Ft​ is known. All the processes we consider will be Ft​-adapted so we will not bother to state this in the sequel.

•

In the continuous-time models that we will study, it will be understood that the filtration {Ft​}t≥0​ will be the filtration generated by the stochastic processes (usually a Brownian motion, Wt​) that are specified in the model description.

1Martingales and Brownian Motion

Definition 1.1. A stochastic process, {Wt​:0≤t≤∞}, is a standard Brownian motion if

1.

W0​=0

2.

It has continuous sample paths

3.

It has independent, normally-distributed increments.

Definition 1.2. An n-dimensional process, Wt​=(Wt(1)​,…,Wt(n)​), is a standard n-dimensional Brownian motion if each Wt(i)​ is a standard Brownian motion and the Wt(i)​’s are independent of each other.

Definition 1.3. A stochastic process, {Xt​ : 0≤t≤∞}, is a martingale with respect to the filtration, Ft​, and probability measure, P, if

1.

EP∣∣Xt​∣∣<∞ for all t≥0

2.

EP[Xt+s​∣Ft​]=Xt​ for all t,s≥0.

Example 1.4. (Brownian martingales) Let Wt​ be a Brownian motion. Then Wt​ , Wt2​−t and exp(θWt​−θ2t/2) are all martingales.

The latter martingale is an example of an exponential martingale. Exponential martingales are of particular significance since they are positive and may be used to define new probability measures.

Example 1.5. (Conditional expectations as martingales) Let Z be a random variable and set Xt​:=E[Z∣Ft​]. Show that Xt​ is a martingale.

2Quadratic Variation

Consider a partition of the time interval, [0,T] given by0=t0​<t1​<t2​<…<tn​=T.Let Xt​ be a Brownian motion and consider the sum of squared changesQn​(T):=i=1∑n​[ΔXti​​]2where ΔXti​​:=Xti​​−Xti−1​​.

Definition 2.1. (Quadratic Variation) The quadratic variation of a stochastic process, Xt​, is equal to the limit of Qn​(T) as Δt:=maxi​(ti​−ti−1​)→0.

Theorem 2.2. The quadratic variation of a Brownian motion is equal to T with probability 1.

The functions with which you are normally familiar, e.g. continuous differentiable functions, have quadratic variation equal to zero. Note that any continuous stochastic process or function that has non-zero quadratic variation must have infinite total variation where the total variation of a process, Xt​, on [0,T] is defined asTotal Variation:=Δt→0lim​i=1∑n​∣Xtk​​−Xtk−1​​∣.This follows by observing thati=1∑n​(Xtk​​−Xtk−1​​)2≤(i=1∑n​∣Xtk​​−Xtk−1​​∣)1≤k≤nmax​∣Xtk​​−Xtk−1​​∣.(1)If we now let n→∞ in (1) then the continuity of Xt​ implies the impossibility of the process having finite total variation and non-zero quadratic variation. Theorem 2.2 therefore implies that the total variation of a Brownian motion is infinite. We have the following important result which will prove very useful when we price options when there are multiple underlying Brownian motions, as is the case with quanto options for example.

Theorem 2.3. (Lévy’s Theorem) A continuous martingale is a Brownian motion if and only if its quadratic variation over each interval [0,t] is equal to t.

Another interesting result is the following:

Theorem 2.4. Any non-constant continuous martingale must have infinite total variation.

We know from our discrete-time models that any arbitrage-free model must have an equivalent martingale measure. The same is true in continuous-time models. Theorem 2.4 then implies that if we work in continuous-time with continuous (deflated) price processes, then these processes must have infinite total variation.

3Stochastic Integrals

We now discuss the concept of a stochastic integral, ignoring the various technical conditions that are required to make our definitions rigorous. In this section, we write Xt​(ω) instead of the usual Xt​ to emphasize that the quantities in question are stochastic.

Definition 3.1. A stopping time of the filtration Ft​ is a random time, τ, such that the event {τ≤t}∈Ft​ for all t>0.

In non-mathematical terms, we see that a stopping time is a random time whose value is part of the information accumulated by that time.

Definition 3.2. We say a process, ht​(ω), is elementary if it is piece-wise constant so that there exists a sequence of stopping times 0=t0​<t1​< … <tn​=T and a set of Fti​​-measurable functions, ei​(ω), such thatht​(ω)=i∑​ei​(ω)I[ti​,ti+1​)​(t)where I[ti​,ti+1​)​(t)=1 if t∈[ti​,ti+1​) and 0 otherwise.

Definition 3.3. The stochastic integral of an elementary function, ht​(ω), with respect to a Brownian motion, Wt​, is defined as∫0T​ht​(ω)dWt​(ω):=i=0∑n−1​ei​(ω)(Wti+1​​(ω)−Wti​​(ω)).(2)

Note that our definition of an elementary function assumes that the function, ht​(ω), is evaluated at the left-hand point of the interval in which t falls. This is a key component in the definition of the stochastic integral: without it the results below would no longer hold. Moreover, defining the stochastic integral in this way makes the resulting theory suitable for financial applications. In particular, if we interpret ht​(ω) as a trading strategy and the stochastic integral as the gains or losses from this trading strategy, then evaluating ht​(ω) at the left-hand point is equivalent to imposing the non-anticipativity of the trading strategy, a property that we always wish to impose.

For a more general process, Xt​(ω), we have∫0T​Xt​(ω)dWt​(ω):=n→∞lim​∫0T​Xt(n)​(ω)dWt​(ω)where Xt(n)​ is a sequence of elementary processes that converges (in an appropriate manner) to Xt​.

Example 3.4. We want to compute ∫0T​Wt​dWt​. Towards this end, let 0=t0n​<t1n​<t2n​<…<tnn​=T be a partition of [0,T] and defineXtn​:=i=0∑n−1​Wtin​​I[tin​,ti+1n​)​(t)where I[tin​,ti+1n​)​(t)=1 if t∈[tin​,ti+1n​) and is 0 otherwise. Then Xtn​ is an adapted elementary process and, by continuity of Brownian motion, satisfies limn→∞​Xtn​=Wt​ almost surely as maxi​∣ti+1n​−tin​∣→0. The Itô integral of Xtn​ is given by∫0T​Xtn​dWt​​=i=0∑n−1​Wtin​​(Wti+1n​​−Wtin​​)=21​i=0∑n−1​(Wti+1n​2​−Wtin​2​−(Wti+1n​​−Wtin​​)2)=21​WT2​−21​W02​−21​i=0∑n−1​(Wti+1n​​−Wtin​​)2.​(3)By the definition of quadratic variation the sum on the right-hand-side of (3) converges in probability to T. And since W0​=0 we obtain∫0T​Wt​dWt​=n→∞lim​∫0T​Xtn​dWt​=21​WT2​−21​T.Note that we will generally evaluate stochastic integrals using Itô’s Lemma (to be discussed later) without having to take limits of elementary processes as we did.

Definition 3.5. We define the space L2[0,T] to be the space of processes, Xt​(ω), such thatE[∫0T​Xt​(ω)2dt]<∞.

Theorem 3.6. (Itô’s Isometry) For any Xt​(ω)∈L2[0,T] we haveE⎣⎡​(∫0T​Xt​(ω)dWt​(ω))2⎦⎤​=E[∫0T​Xt​(ω)2dt].

证明. (For the case where Xt​ is an elementary process) Let Xt​=∑i​ei​(ω)I[ti​,ti+1​)​(t) be an elementary process where the ei​(ω)’s and ti​’s are as defined in Definition 3.2. We therefore have ∫0T​Xt​(ω)dWt​(ω):=∑i=0n−1​ei​(ω)(Wti+1​​(ω)−Wti​​(ω)). We then have​E⎣⎡​(∫0T​Xt​(ω)dWt​(ω))2⎦⎤​=E⎣⎡​(i=0∑n−1​ei​(ω)(Wti+1​​(ω)−Wti​​(ω)))2⎦⎤​=i=0∑n−1​E[ei2​(ω)(Wti+1​​(ω)−Wti​​(ω))2]+20≤i<j≤n−1∑n−1​E[ei​ej​(ω)(Wti+1​​(ω)−Wti​​(ω))(Wtj+1​​(ω)−Wtj​​(ω))]=i=0∑n−1​E⎣⎡​ei2​(ω)=ti+1​−ti​Eti​​[(Wti+1​​(ω)−Wti​​(ω))2]​​⎦⎤​+20≤i<j≤n−1∑n−1​E⎣⎡​ei​ej​(ω)(Wti+1​​(ω)−Wti​​(ω))=0Etj​​[(Wtj+1​​(ω)−Wtj​​(ω))]​​⎦⎤​=E[i=0∑n−1​ei2​(ω)(ti+1​−ti​)]=E[∫0T​Xt​(ω)2dt]​which is what we had to show.

□

Theorem 3.7. (Martingale Property of Stochastic Integrals) The stochastic integral, Yt​:=∫0t​Xs​(ω)dWs​(ω), is a martingale for any Xt​(ω)∈L2[0,T].

Example 3.8. Check that ∫0t​Xs​(ω)dWt​(ω) is indeed a martingale when Xt​ is an elementary process.

4Stochastic Differential Equations

Definition 4.1. An n-dimensional Itô process, Xt​, is a process that can be represented asXt​=X0​+∫0t​as​ds+∫0t​bs​dWs​(4)where W is an m-dimensional standard Brownian motion, and a and b are n-dimensional and n×m-dimensional Ft​-adapted processes, respectively.

We often use the notationdXt​=at​dt+bt​dWt​as shorthand for (4). An n-dimensional stochastic differential equation (SDE) has the formdXt​=a(Xt​,t)dt+b(Xt​,t)dWt​;X0​=x(5)where as before, Wt​ is an m-dimensional standard Brownian motion, and a and b are n-dimensional and n×m-dimensional adapted processes, respectively. Once again, (5) is shorthand forXt​=x+∫0t​a(Xs​,s)dt+∫0t​b(Xs​,t)dWs​.(6)While we do not discuss the issue here, various conditions exist to guarantee existence and uniqueness of solutions to (6). A useful tool for solving SDE’s is Itô’s Lemma which we now discuss.

5Itô’s Lemma

Itô’s Lemma is the most important result in stochastic calculus, the "sine qua non" of the field. We first state and give an outline proof of a basic form of the result.

Theorem 5.1. (Itô’s Lemma for 1-dimensional Brownian Motion) Let Wt​ be a Brownian motion on [0,T] and suppose f(x) is a twice continuously differentiable function on R. Then for any t≤T we havef(Wt​)=f(0)+21​∫0t​f′′(Ws​)ds+∫0t​f′(Ws​)dWs​.(7)

证明. (Sketch) Let 0=t0​<t1​<t2​<…<tn​=t be a partition of [0,t]. Clearlyf(Wt​)=f(0)+i=0∑n−1​(f(Wti+1​​)−f(Wti​​)).(8)Taylor’s Theorem impliesf(Wti+1​​)−f(Wti​​)=f′(Wti​​)(Wti+1​​−Wti​​)+21​f′′(θi​)(Wti+1​​−Wti​​)2(9)for some θi​∈(Wti​​,Wti+1​​). Substituting (9) into (8) we obtainf(Wt​)=f(0)+i=0∑n−1​f′(Wti​​)(Wti+1​​−Wti​​)+21​i=0∑n−1​f′′(θi​)(Wti+1​​−Wti​​)2.(10)If we let δ:=maxi​∣ti+1​−ti​∣→0 then it can be shown that the terms on the right-hand-side of (10) converge to the corresponding terms on the right-hand-side of (7) as desired. (This should not be surprising as we know the quadratic variation of Brownian motion on [0,t] is equal to t.)

□

A more general version of Itô’s Lemma can be stated for Itô processes.

Theorem 5.2. (Itô’s Lemma for 1-dimensional Itô process) Let Xt​ be a 1-dimensional Itô process satisfying the SDEdXt​=μt​dt+σt​dWt​.If f(t,x):[0,∞)×R→R is a C1,2 function and Zt​:=f(t,Xt​) thendZt​​=∂t∂f​(t,Xt​)dt+∂x∂f​(t,Xt​)dXt​+21​∂x2∂2f​(t,Xt​)(dXt​)2=(∂t∂f​(t,Xt​)+∂x∂f​(t,Xt​)μt​+21​∂x2∂2f​(t,Xt​)σt2​)dt+∂x∂f​(t,Xt​)σt​dWt​.​

The "Box" Calculus

In the statement of Itô’s Lemma, we implicitly assumed that (dXt​)2=σt2​dt. The "box calculus" is a series of simple rules for calculating such quantities. In particular, we use the rulesdt×dt=dt×dWt​=0anddWt​×dWt​=dtwhen determining quantities such as (dXt​)2 in the statement of Itô’s Lemma above. Note that these rules are consistent with Theorem 2.2. When we have two correlated Brownian motions, Wt(1)​ and Wt(2)​, with correlation coefficient, ρt​, then we easily obtain that dWt(1)​×dWt(2)​=ρt​dt. We use the box calculus for computing the quadratic variation of Itô processes.

Example 5.3. Let Wt(1)​ and Wt(2)​ be two independent Brownian motions. Use Lévy’s Theorem to show thatWt​:=ρWt(1)​+1−ρ2​Wt(2)​is also a Brownian motion for a given constant, ρ.

Example 5.4. Suppose a stock price, St​, satisfies the SDEdSt​=μt​St​dt+σt​St​dWt​.Then we can use the substitution, Yt​=log(St​) and Itô’s Lemma applied to the function f(x):=log(x) to obtainSt​=S0​exp(∫0t​(μs​−σs2​/2)ds+∫0t​σs​dWs​).(11)Note that St​ does not appear on the right-hand-side of (11) so that we have indeed solved the SDE. When μs​=μ and σs​=σ are constants we obtainSt​=S0​exp((μ−σ2/2)t+σdWt​)(12)so that log(St​)∼N((μ−σ2/2)t,σ2t).

Example 5.5. (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process) Let St​ be a security price and suppose Xt​=log(St​) satisfies the SDEdXt​=[−γ(Xt​−μt)+μ]dt+σdWt​.Then we can apply Itô’s Lemma to Yt​:=exp(γt)Xt​ to obtaindYt​​=exp(γt)dXt​+Xt​d(exp(γt))=exp(γt)([−γ(Xt​−μt)+μ]dt+σdWt​)+Xt​γexp(γt)dt=exp(γt)([γμt+μ]dt+σdWt​)​so thatYt​=Y0​+μ∫0t​eγs(γs+1)ds+σ∫0t​eγsdWs​(13)or alternatively (after simplifying the Riemann integral in (13))Xt​=X0​e−γt+μt+σe−γt∫0t​eγsdWs​.(14)Once again, note that Xt​ does not appear on the right-hand-side of (14) so that we have indeed solved the SDE. We also obtain E[Xt​]=X0​e−γt+μt andVar(Xt​)​=Var(σe−γt∫0t​eγsdWs​)=σ2e−2γtE[(∫0t​eγsdWs​)2]=σ2e−2γt∫0t​e2γsds(by Itoˆ’s Isometry)=2γσ2​(1−e−2γt).​(15)These moments should be compared with the corresponding moments for log(St​) in the previous example.

Theorem 5.6. (Itô’s Lemma for n-dimensional Itô process) Let Xt​ be an n-dimensional Itô process satisfying the SDEdXt​=μt​dt+σt​dWt​.where Xt​∈Rn, μt​∈Rn, σt​∈Rn×m and Wt​ is a standard m-dimensional Brownian motion. If f(t,x):[0,∞)×Rn→R is a C1,2 function and Zt​:=f(t,Xt​) thendZt​=∂t∂f​(t,Xt​)dt+i∑​∂xi​∂f​(t,Xt​)dXt(i)​+21​i,j∑​∂xi​∂xj​∂2f​(t,Xt​)dXt(i)​dXt(j)​where dWt(i)​dWt(j)​=dtdWt(i)​=0 for i=j and dWt(i)​dWt(i)​=dt.

Example 5.7. Let Xt​ and Yt​ satisfydXt​dYt​​=μt(1)​dt+σt(1,1)​dWt(1)​=μt(2)​dt+σt(2,1)​dWt(1)​+σt(2,2)​dWt(2)​​and define Zt​:=Xt​Yt​. Apply the multi-dimensional version of Itô’s Lemma to find the SDE satisfied by Zt​.

6The Martingale Representation Theorem

The martingale representation theorem is an important result that is particularly useful for constructing replicating portfolios in complete financial models.

Theorem 6.1. Suppose Mt​ is an Ft​-martingale where {Ft​}t≥0​ is the filtration generated by the n-dimensional standard Brownian motion, Wt​=(Wt(1)​,…,Wt(n)​). If E[Mt2​]<∞ for all t then there exists a unique n-dimensional adapted stochastic process, ϕt​, such thatMt​=M0​+∫0t​ϕsT​dWt​ for all t≥0where ϕsT​ denotes the transpose of the vector, ϕs​.

Example 6.2. Let F=WT3​ and define Mt​=Et​[F]. We will show thatMt​=3∫0t​(T−s+Ws2​)dWs​(16)which is consistent with the Martingale Representation theorem. First we must calculate Mt​. We do this using the independent increments property of Brownian motion and obtainMt​​=Et​[WT3​]=Et​[(WT​−Wt​+Wt​)3]==0Et​[(WT​−Wt​)3]​​+Et​[Wt3​]+3Et​[Wt​(WT​−Wt​)2]+=03Et​[Wt2​(WT​−Wt​)]​​=Wt3​+3Wt​(T−t).(17)​We can now apply Itô’s Lemma to (17) to obtaindMt​​=3Wt2​dWt​+21​⋅6Wt​dt+3(T−t)dWt​−3Wt​dt=3(Wt2​+T−t)dWt​​which, noting M0​=0, is (16).

7Gaussian Processes

Definition 7.1. A process Xt​, t≥0, is a Gaussian process if (Xt1​​,…,Xtn​​) is jointly normally distributed for every n and every set of times 0≤t1​≤t2​≤…≤tn​.

If Xt​ is a Gaussian process, then it is determined by its mean function, m(t), and its covariance function, ρ(s,t), wherem(t)ρ(s,t)​=E[Xt​]=E[(Xs​−m(s))(Xt​−m(t))].​In particular, the joint moment generating function (MGF) of (Xt1​​,…,Xtn​​) is given byMt1​,…,tn​​(θ1​,…,θn​)=exp(θTm(t)+21​θTΣθ)(18)where m(t)=(m(t1​)…m(tn​))T and Σi,j​=ρ(ti​,tj​).

Example 7.2. (Brownian motion) Brownian motion is a Gaussian process with m(t)=0 and ρ(s,t)=min(s,t) for all s,t≥0.

Theorem 7.3. (Integration of a deterministic function w.r.t. a Brownian motion) Let Wt​ be a Brownian motion and supposeXt​=∫0t​δs​dWs​where δs​ is a deterministic function. Then Xt​ is a Gaussian process with m(t)=0 and ρ(s,t)=∫0min(s,t)​δs2​ds.

证明. (Sketch) (1) First use Itô’s Lemma to show thatE[euXt​]=1+21​u2∫0t​δs2​E[euXs​]ds.(19)If we set yt​:=E[euXt​] then we can differentiate across (19) to obtain the ODEdtdy​=21​u2δt2​y.This is easily solved to obtain the MGF for Xt​,E[euXt​]=exp(21​u2∫0t​δs2​ds)(20)which, as expected, is the MGF of a normal random variable with mean 0 and variance ∫0t​δs2​ds.

(2) We now use (20) and similar computations to show that the joint MGF of (Xt1​​,…,Xtn​​) has the form given in (18) with m(t)=0 and ρ(s,t)=∫0min(s,t)​δs2​ds. (See Shreve’s Stochastic Calculus for Finance II for further details.)

□

The next theorem again concerns Gaussian processes and is often of interest when studying short-rate term structure models.

Theorem 7.4. Let Wt​ be a Brownian motion and suppose δt​ and ϕt​ are deterministic functions. IfXt​:=∫0t​δu​dWu​ and Yt​:=∫0t​ϕu​Xu​duthen Yt​ is a Gaussian process with m(t)=0 andρ(s,t)=∫0min(s,t)​δv2​(∫vs​ϕy​dy)(∫vt​ϕy​dy)dv.

证明. The proof is tedious but straightforward. (Again, see Shreve’s Stochastic Calculus for Finance II for further details.)

□

Note for example that Brownian motion with drift and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process are both Gaussian processes. Nonetheless, we saw in Example 5.5 that these two processes behave very differently: the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process mean-reverts and its variance tends to a finite limit as T→∞. This is not true of Brownian motion with or without drift.

8The Feynman-Kac Formula

Suppose Xt​ is a scalar stochastic process satisfying the SDEdXt​=μ(t,Xt​)dt+σ(t,Xt​)dWt​(21)where as usual μ(t,Xt​) and σ(t,Xt​) are Ft​-adapted and satisfy sufficient conditions to guarantee existence of a unique solution to (21). Now consider the function, f(x,t), given byf(t,x)=Etx​[∫tT​ϕs(t)​h(Xs​,s)ds+ϕT(t)​g(XT​)]whereϕs(t)​=exp(−∫ts​r(Xu​,u)du)and the notation Etx​[⋅] implies that the expectation should be taken conditional on time t information with Xt​=x. Note that f(x,t) may be interpreted as the time t price of a security that pays dividends at a continuous rate, h(Xs​,s) for s≥t, and with a terminal payoff g(XT​) at time T. Of course E[⋅] should then be interpreted as an expectation under an equivalent martingale measure with the cash account as the corresponding numeraire and r(⋅,⋅) as the instantaneous risk-free rate.

The Feynman-Kac Theorem states that f(⋅,⋅) satisfies the following PDE∂t∂f​(t,Xt​)+∂x∂f​(t,Xt​)μt​(t,Xt​)+21​∂x2∂2f​(t,Xt​)σt2​(t,Xt​)−r(x,t)f(x,t)+h(x,t)f(x,T)​=0,(x,t)∈R×[0,T)=g(x),x∈R​

证明. (Sketch proof) We will use the martingale property of conditional expectations which states that if Mt​:=Et​[F] where F is a given fixed random variable then Mt​ is a martingale. First letf(t,Xt​):=Et​[∫tT​ϕs(t)​h(Xs​,s)ds+ϕT(t)​g(XT​)](22)and note that the random variable inside the expectation on the right-hand-side of (22) is a function of t. This means we cannot yet apply the martingale property of conditional expectations. However by adding ∫0t​ϕs(t)​h(Xs​,s)ds to both sides of (22) and then multiplying both sides by ϕt(0)​ we obtainϕt(0)​(f(t,Xt​)+∫0t​ϕs(t)​h(Xs​,s)ds)​=Et​[∫0T​ϕs(0)​h(Xs​,s)ds+ϕT(0)​g(XT​)]=Et​[Z],say.​Note that Z does not depend on t and so we can now apply the martingale property of conditional expectations to conclude that the left-hand-side is a martingale. We therefore apply Itô’s Lemma to the left-hand-side and set the coefficient of dt to zero. This results in the Feynman-Kac PDE given above.

□

Remark 8.1. The Feynman-Kac result generalizes easily to the case where Xt​ is an n-dimensional Itô process driven by an m-dimensional standard Brownian motion.

The Feynman-Kac Theorem plays an important role in financial engineering as it enables us to compute the prices of derivative securities (which can be expressed as expectations according to martingale pricing theory) by solving a PDE instead. It is worth mentioning, however, that in the development of derivatives pricing theory, the PDE approach preceded the martingale approach. Indeed by constructing a replicating strategy for a given derivative security, it can be shown directly that the price of the derivative security satisfies the Feynman-Kac PDE.

9The Kolmogorov Equations

We assume in this section that Xt​ again satisfies the SDE of (21). Letu(x,t):=E[Φ(Xs​)∣Xt​=x]for some function Φ(⋅) and with s>t. Then following the same argument that we used in Section 8 we see that u satisfiesut​+μ(t,x)ux​+21​σ2(t,x)uxx​=0 for t<s  with u(x,s)=Φ(x).(23)Suppose we now takeΦ(x)={1,0,​for x≤yotherwise.​so that u(x,t)=P(Xs​≤y∣Xt​=x)=:P(t,x;s,y), say. Let p(t,x;s,y) be the corresponding PDF so that p(t,x;s,y)=∂P(t,x;s,y)/∂y. By (formally) differentiating across (23) with respect to y we obtain Kolmogorov’s backward equation for the transition density, p(t,x;s,y). In particular we obtainpt​+μ(t,x)px​+21​σ2(t,x)pxx​=0 for t<s.(Kolmogorov’s Backward Equation)(24)It is worth emphasizing that (24) does not always admit a unique solution. In particular boundary conditions need to be specified. For example absorbing and reflecting Brownian motions both satisfy (24) but they are very different processes. It is also worth mentioning that (23) itself is what people sometimes have in mind when they refer to Kolmogorov’s backward equation.

In order to state Kolmogorov’s forward equation we must now view p(t,x;s,y) as a function of (s,y) and therefore keep (t,x) fixed. It can be shown thatps​+(μ(s,y)p)y​−21​(σ2(t,y)p)yy​=0 for s>t.(Kolmogorov’s Forward Equation)(25)with the initial condition p=δx​(y) at s=t. The forward equation can be derived quickly in a formal manner from the backward equation using integration by parts but doing so rigorously can be very challenging. In fact, depending on technical and boundary conditions the forward equation (25) may not actually be satisfied. The forward equation plays a key role in local volatility models of security prices where it is used to derive the Dupire formula.

10Change of Probability Measure

The majority of financial engineering models price securities using the EMM, Q, that corresponds to taking the cash account, Bt​, as numeraire. Sometimes, however, it is particularly useful to work with another numeraire, Nt​, and its corresponding EMM, PN​ say. We now describe how to create new probability measures and how to switch back and forth between these measures.

Let Q be a given probability measure and Mt​ a strictly positive Q-martingale such that E0Q​[Mt​]=1 for all t∈[0,T]. We may then define a new equivalent probability measure, PM, by definingPM​(A)=EQ[MT​1A​].Note that

(i)

PM​(Ω)=1

(ii)

PM​(A)≥0 for every event A and

(iii)

It can easily be shown that PM​(i⋃​Ai​)=i∑​PM​(Ai​)whenever the Ai​’s form a sequence of disjoint sets.

Points (i), (ii) and (iii) above imply that PM​ is indeed a probability measure. Because the null-sets of Q and PM​ coincide we can conclude that PM​ is indeed an equivalent probability measure (to Q). Expectations with respect to PM​ then satisfyE0PM​​[X]=E0Q​[MT​X].(26)

Example 10.1. Verify (26) in the case where X(ω)=∑i=1n​ci​I{ω∈Ai​}​, MT​ is constant on each Ai​, and where A1​,…,An​ form a partition of Ω.

When we define a measure change this way, we use the notation dPM​/dQ to refer to MT​ so that we often writedQdPM​​=MT​.

The following result explains how to switch between Q and PM​ when we are taking conditional expectations. In particular, we haveEtPM​​[X]​=EtQ​[dQdPM​​]EtQ​[dQdPM​​X]​(27)=Mt​EtQ​[dQdPM​​X]​.(28)​

Since Mt​ is a Q-martingale (28) follows easily from (27). We defer a proof of (27) to Appendix A as it requires the measure-theoretic definition of a conditional expectation.

We need to show that (27) is true. That is, we must showEtPM​​[X]=EtQ​[dQdPM​​]EtQ​[dQdPM​​X]​.(*)To do this we first recall the definition of a conditional expectation. This definition states that Y is the PM​-expected value of X conditional on Ft​ if Y is an Ft​-measurable random variable satisfyingEPM​[ξX]=EPM​[ξY]for all bounded Ft​-measurable random variables, ξ. Y is then typically written as EPM​[X∣Ft​]≡EtPM​​[X]. We are now in a position to prove (*). First note that the right-hand-side of (39) is indeed Ft​-measurable, as required. Now let ξ be Ft​-measurable. We then haveEPM​⎣⎡​EtQ​[dQdPM​​]EtQ​[XdQdPM​​]​ξ⎦⎤​​=EQ⎣⎡​EtQ​[dQdPM​​]EtQ​[XdQdPM​​]​ξdQdPM​​⎦⎤​=EQ⎣⎡​EtQ​[dQdPM​​]EtQ​[XdQdPM​​]​ξEtQ​[dQdPM​​]⎦⎤​=EQ[EtQ​[XdQdPM​​ξ]]=EQ[XdQdPM​​ξ]=EPM​[Xξ]​and so (*) holds.

Example 10.2. Show that if X is Ft​-measurable, i.e. X is known by time t, then E0PM​​[X]=E0Q​[Mt​X].

Remark 10.3. Since MT​ is strictly positive we can set X=IA​/MT​ in (26) where IA​ is the indicator function of the event A. We then obtain E0PM​​[IA​/MT​]=E0Q​[IA​]=Q(A). In particular, we see that dQ/dPM​ is given by 1/MT​.

Remark 10.4. In the context of security pricing, we can take Mt​ to be the deflated time t price of a security with strictly positive payoff, normalized so that its expectation under Q is equal to 1. For example, let ZtT​ be the time t price of a zero-coupon bond maturing at time T, and let Bt​ denote the time t value of the cash account. We could then set MT​:=1/(BT​Z0T​) so thatMt​=EtQ​[BT​Z0T​1​]is indeed a Q-martingale. The resulting measure, denoted by PT​, is sometimes called the T-forward measure. Note that we have implicitly assumed that in this context, Q refers to the EMM when we take the cash account as numeraire. We discuss PT​ in further detail in Section 11.

11A Useful EMM: The Forward Measure

We now discuss the τ-forward measure, Pτ, which is the EMM that corresponds to taking the zero-coupon bond with maturity τ as the numeraire. We therefore let Ztτ​ denote the time t price of a zero-coupon bond maturing at time τ≥t and with face value $1. As usual, we let Q denote the EMM corresponding to taking the cash account, Bt​, as numeraire. We assume without loss of generality that B0​=$1 and now use Ztτ​ to define our new measure. To do this, setdQdPτ​=Bτ​Z0τ​1​.(29)

Example 11.1. Check that (29) does indeed define an equivalent probability measure.

Now let Ct​ denote the time t price of a contingent claim that expires at time τ. We then haveCt​​=Bt​EtQ​[Bτ​Cτ​​](by martingale pricing with EMM Q)(30)=EtPτ​[Bτ​Z0τ​]Bt​EtPτ​[Bτ​Cτ​​Bτ​Z0τ​]​(going from Q to Pτ using (27))(31)=EtQ​[1]/EtQ​[1/(Bτ​Z0τ​)]Bt​Z0τ​EtPτ​[Cτ​]​(going from Pτ to Q in the denominator of (31) using (27))=Ztτ​EtPτ​[Cτ​](by martingale pricing with EMM Q).(32)​

We can now find Ct​, either through equation (32) or through equation (30) where we use the cash account as numeraire. Computing Ct​ through (30) is our "usual method" and is often very convenient. When pricing equity derivatives, for example, we usually take interest rates, and hence the cash account, to be deterministic. This means that the factor 1/Bτ​ in (30) can be taken outside the expectation so only the Q-distribution of Cτ​ is needed to compute Ct​.

When interest rates are stochastic we cannot take the factor 1/Bτ​ outside the expectation in (30) and we therefore need to find the joint Q-distribution of (Bτ​,Cτ​) in order to compute Ct​. On the other hand, if we use equation (32) to compute Ct​, then we only need the Pτ-distribution of Cτ​, regardless of whether or not interest rates are stochastic. Working with a univariate-distribution is generally much easier than working with a bivariate-distribution so if we can easily find the Pτ-distribution of Cτ​, then it can often be very advantageous to work with this distribution. The forward measure is therefore particularly useful when studying term-structure models.

Switching to a different numeraire can also be advantageous in other circumstances, even when interest rates are deterministic. For example, we will find it convenient to do so when pricing quanto-options and options on multiple underlying securities. Moreover, we will see how we can use Girsanov’s Theorem to move back and forth between Q and other EMMs corresponding to other numeraires.

12Girsanov’s Theorem

Girsanov’s Theorem is one of the most important results for financial engineering applications. When working with models driven by Brownian motions it enables us to (i) identify the equivalent martingale measure(s) corresponding to a given numeraire and (ii) to move back and forth between different EMM-numeraire pairs. Consider then the processLt​:=exp(−∫0t​ηs​dWs​−21​∫0t​ηs2​ds)(33)where ηs​ is an adapted process and Ws​ is a P-Brownian motion. Using Itô’s Lemma we can check that dLt​=−Lt​ηt​dWt​ so Lt​ is a positive martingale with E0P​[Lt​]=1 for all t.

Theorem 12.1. (Girsanov’s Theorem) Define an equivalent probability measure, Qη, by settingQη(A):=E0P​[LT​1A​].(34)Then Wt​:=Wt​+∫0t​ηs​ds is a standard Qη-Brownian motion. Moreover, Wt​ has the martingale representation property under Qη.

Remark 12.2. Suppose ηs​=η, a constant. Then since Wt​:=Wt​+ηt is a standard Qη-Brownian motion, it implies that Wt​=Wt​−ηt is a Qη-Brownian motion with drift −η.

Example 12.3. Let dXt​=μt​dt+σt​dWt​ and suppose we wish to find a process, ηs​, such that Xt​ is a Qη-martingale. This is easily achieved as follows:dXt​​=μt​dt+σt​dWt​=μt​dt+σt​(dWt​−ηt​dt)=σt​dWt​​if we set ηt​=μt​/σt​ in which case Xt​ is a Qη-martingale. We can obtain some intuition for this result: suppose for example that μt​ and σt​ are both positive so that ηt​ is also positive. Then we can see from the definition of Lt​ in (33) that Lt​ places less weight on paths where Wt​ drifts upwards than it does on paths where it drifts downwards. This relative weighting adjusts Xt​ for the positive drift induced by μt​ with the result that under Qη, Xt​ is a martingale.

Remark 12.4. Note that Girsanov’s Theorem enables us to compute Qη-expectations directly without having to switch back to the original measure, P.

We can get some additional intuition for the Girsanov Theorem by considering a random walk, X={X0​=0,X1​,…,Xn​} with the interpretation that Xi​ is the value of the walk at time iT/n. In particular, Xn​ corresponds to the value of the random walk at time T. We assume that ΔXi​:=Xi​−Xi−1​∼N(0,T/n) under P and is independent of X0​,…,Xi−1​ for i=1,…n.

Example 12.5. Suppose now that we want to compute θ:=E0Q​[h(X)] where Q denotes the probability measure under which ΔXi​∼N(μ,T/n), again independently of X0​,…,Xi−1​. In particular, if we set μ:=−Tη/n then Xt​ approximates standard Brownian motion under P and Xt​ approximates Brownian motion with drift −η under Q. If we let f(⋅) and g(⋅) denote the PDF’s of N(μ,T/n) and N(0,T/n) random variables, respectively, then we obtainθ​=E0Q​[h(X)]=∫Rn​h(x1​,…,xn​)(i=1∏n​f(Δxi​))dΔx1​…dΔxn​=∫Rn​h(x1​,…,xn​)i∏​(g(Δxi​)f(Δxi​)​g(Δxi​))dΔx1​…dΔxn​=∫Rn​h(x1​,…,xn​)i∏​(g(Δxi​)f(Δxi​)​)(i∏​g(Δxi​))dΔx1​…dΔxn​=E0P​[h(X1​,…,Xn​)i∏​(g(ΔXi​)f(ΔXi​)​)]=E0P​[h(X1​,…,Xn​)exp(−ηi∑​ΔXi​−2η2T​)]=E0P​[h(X1​,…,Xn​)exp(−ηXn​−2η2T​)]​which is consistent with our statement of Girsanov’s Theorem in (33) and (34) above. (See Remark 4.)

Remark 12.6. (i) As in the statement of the Girsanov Theorem itself, we could have chosen μ (and therefore η) to be adapted, i.e. to depend on prior events, in the random walk.

(ii) Note that Girsanov’s Theorem allows the drift, but not the volatility of the Brownian motion, to change under the new measure, Qη. It is interesting to see that we are not so constrained in the case of the random walk. Have you any intuition for why this is so?

Multidimensional Girsanov’s Theorem

The multidimensional version of Girsanov’s Theorem is a straightforward generalization of the one-dimensional version. In particular let Wt​ be an n-dimensional standard P-Brownian motion and defineLt​:=exp(−∫0t​ηsT​dWs​−21​∫0t​ηsT​ηs​ds)for t∈[0,T]. Then Wt​:=Wt​+∫0t​ηs​ds is a standard Qη-Brownian motion where dQη/dP=LT​.

13An Application: Martingale Pricing Theory

We now briefly outline how the martingale pricing theory that we have seen in a discrete-time, discrete-space framework translates to a continuous-time setting. We use St​ to denote the time t price of a risky asset and Bt​ to denote the time t value of the cash account. For ease of exposition we will initially assume that the risky asset does not pay dividends. Let ϕt(s)​ and ϕt(b)​ denote the number of units of the security and cash account, respectively, that is held in a portfolio at time t. Then the value of the portfolio at time t is given byVt​=ϕt(s)​St​+ϕt(b)​Bt​.

Definition 13.1. We say ϕt​:=(ϕt(s)​,ϕt(b)​) is self-financing ifdVt​=ϕt(s)​dSt​+ϕt(b)​dBt​.

Note that this definition is consistent with our definition for discrete-time models. It is also worth emphasizing the mathematical content of this definition. Note that Itô’s Lemma impliesdVt​=ϕt(s)​dSt​+ϕt(b)​dBt​+ASt​dϕt(s)​+Bt​dϕt(b)​​​+dSt​dϕt(s)​+dBt​dϕt(b)​so that the self-financing assumption amounts to assuming that the sum of the terms in A are identically zero. Our definitions of arbitrage, numeraire securities, equivalent martingale measures and complete markets is unchanged from the discrete-time setup. We now state without proof the two fundamental theorems of asset pricing. These results mirror those from the discrete-time theory.

Theorem 13.2. (The First Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing) There is no arbitrage if and only if there exists an EMM, Q.

A consequence of Theorem 13.2 is that in the absence of arbitrage, the deflated value process, Vt​/Nt​, of any self-financing trading strategy is a Q-martingale. This implies that the deflated price of any attainable security can be computed as the Q-expectation of the terminal deflated value of the security.

Theorem 13.3. (The Second Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing) Assume there exists a security with strictly positive price process and that there are no arbitrage opportunities. Then the market is complete if and only if there exists exactly one risk-neutral martingale measure, Q.

Beyond their theoretical significance, these theorems are also important in practice. If our model is complete then we can price securities with the unique EMM that accompanies it, assuming of course the absence of arbitrage. This is the case for the Black-Scholes model as well as local volatility models. If our model is incomplete then we generally work directly under an EMM, Q, which is then calibrated to market data. In particular, the true data-generating probability measure, P, is often completely ignored when working with incomplete models. In some sense the issue of completeness then only arises when we discuss replicating or hedging strategies.

Determining Replicating Strategies

The following example is particularly useful in many financial engineering applications. While we focus on the case of a single risky security the result generalizes easily to multiple risky securities. We assume the market is complete of course, since only in that case can we guarantee that a replicating strategy actually exists.

Example 13.4. (Wealth Dynamics and Hedging) We know the value of the cash-account, Bt​, satisfies dBt​=rt​Bt​dt and suppose in addition that St​ satisfiesdSt​=μt​St​dt+σt​St​dWt​.(35)Then for a portfolio (ϕt(s)​,ϕt(b)​), the portfolio value, Vt​, at time t satisfies Vt​:=ϕt(s)​St​+ϕt(b)​Bt​. If ϕt​:=(ϕt(s)​,ϕt(b)​) is self-financing, then we havedVt​​=ϕt(s)​dSt​+ϕt(b)​dBt​=ϕt(s)​μt​St​dt+ϕt(s)​σt​St​dWt​+ϕt(b)​rt​Bt​dt=Vt​[Vt​ϕt(s)​St​​μt​+Vt​ϕt(b)​Bt​​rt​]dt+Vt​ϕt(s)​St​​σt​Vt​dWt​=Vt​[rt​+θt​(μt​−rt​)]dt+θt​σt​Vt​dWt​​where θt​ and (1−θt​) are the fractions of time t wealth, Vt​, invested in the risky asset and cash account, respectively, at time t.

Suppose now that Vt​ is the time t value of some derivative security and that we want to determine the self-financing trading strategy, (ϕt(s)​,ϕt(b)​), that replicates it. By using Itô’s Lemma to write the dynamics of Vt​ as in (35), we can immediately determine θt​, the fraction of time t wealth that is invested in the risky asset. In particular, θt​ is the coefficient of σt​Vt​dWt​ in the dynamics of Vt​. Note also that we can work under any probability measure we choose since different probability measures will only change the drift of Vt​ and not the volatility. Once we have θt​ we immediately have 1−θt​ and then also (ϕt(s)​,ϕt(b)​).

Remark 13.5. If a security pays dividends or coupons, then in the above statements we should replace the security price with the total gain process from holding the security. For example, if a stock pays a continuous dividend yield of q, then Yt​:=eqtSt​ is the total gain process. It is what your portfolio would be worth at time t if you purchased one unit of the security at time t=0 and reinvested all dividends immediately back into the stock. The portfolio (ϕt(y)​,ϕt(b)​) is then said to be self-financing ifdVt​​=ϕt(y)​dYt​+ϕt(b)​dBt​=ϕt(y)​d(eqtSt​)+ϕt(b)​dBt​=ϕt(y)​(eqtdSt​+qYt​dt)+ϕt(b)​dBt​=ϕt(s)​(dSt​+qSt​dt)+ϕt(b)​dBt​​(36)where ϕt(s)​=eqtϕt(y)​ is the number of units of the risky asset held at time t. We shall make use of (36) when we price options on dividend-paying securities.

The Role of Girsanov’s Theorem

Suppose we again adopt the setting of Example 13.4 and that the risky security does not pay dividends. If we deflate as usual by the cash account then we can let Zt​:=St​/Bt​ denote the deflated time t value of the risky asset. Assume also that Wt​ is a P-Brownian motion where P is the true data-generating probability measure. Then it is easy to check using Itô’s Lemma thatdZt​=Zt​(μt​−r)dt+Zt​σt​dWt​.(37)But we know from the first fundamental theorem that Zt​ must be a Q-martingale. Girsanov’s Theorem, however, implies that Zt​ is a Q-martingale only if Wt​:=Wt​+∫0t​ηs​ds is a Q-Brownian motion with ηs​:=(μs​−r)/σs​. Indeed, because there is only one such process, ηs​, this Q is unique and the market is therefore complete by the second fundamental theorem. We then obtain that the Q-dynamics for St​ satisfydSt​=rSt​dt+σt​St​dWt​.

Example 13.6. Suppose now that the risky asset pays a continuous dividend yield, q. Show that the Q-dynamics of St​ now satisfydSt​=(r−q)St​dt+σt​St​dWt​.(Hint: Remember that it is now the deflated total gains process that is now a Q-martingale.)

We can use these observations now to derive the Black-Scholes formula. Suppose the stock-price, St​, has P-dynamicsdSt​=μt​St​dt+σSt​dWt​where Wt​ is a P-Brownian motion. Note that we have now assumed a constant volatility, σ, as Black and Scholes originally assumed. If the stock pays a continuous dividend yield of q then martingale pricing implies that the price of a call option on the stock with maturity T and strike K is given byC0​=E0Q​[e−rT(ST​−K)+](38)where log(ST​)∼N((r−q−σ2/2)T,σT). We can therefore compute the right-hand-side of (38) analytically to obtain the Black-Scholes formula.

Example 13.7. Consider an equity model with two non dividend-paying securities, A and B, whose price processes, St(a)​ and St(b)​ respectively, satisfy the following SDE’sdSt(a)​dSt(b)​​=rSt(a)​dt+σ1​St(a)​dWt(1)​=rSt(b)​dt+σ2​St(b)​(ρdWt(1)​+1−ρ2​dWt(2)​)​where (Wt(1)​,Wt(2)​) is a 2-dimensional Q-standard Brownian motion. We assume the cash account is the numeraire security corresponding to Q (which is consistent with the Q-dynamics of St(a)​ and St(b)​) and that the continuously compounded interest rate, r, is constant. Use the change of numeraire technique to compute the time 0 price, C0​ of a European option that expires at time T with payoff max(0,ST(a)​−ST(b)​). (We will have plenty of practice with Girsanov’s Theorem and changing probability measures as the course progresses.)

14The Remaining Items: PDE Pricing Method

The Black-Scholes model postulates that the stock price St​ is described by a geometric Brownian motion:dSt​=αSt​dt+σSt​dWto​,or St​=S0​e(α−21​σ2)t+σWto​.Here Wto​ is a Brownian motion process defined on a probability space (Ω,F,Po). The parameter σ is the volatility and α is the mean rate of growth. The market also has a risk-free asset or ”bond” with constant interest rate r:dBt​=rBt​dt,or Bt​=B0​ert.

This model originated with the work of Black, Scholes and Merton. Its shortcomings as a model of the real market have been discussed in the literature, and various modifications have been considered. Our purpose is not to decide on the most accurate model. Without intending to diminish their importance, we are not covering models involving multiple stocks, state-dependent or stochastic volatility, incomplete markets, regime switching, jump-diffusions, or Lévy processes. Nor are we considering model calibration or parameter estimation. Instead our purpose is to use the the simple Black-Scholes model as a ”laboratory” in which to learn various techniques for calculating the prices of financial derivatives based on the no-arbitrage principle. The methods we learn here can be adapted to more complex models, though we will not pursue that.

No-Arbitrage and Risk-Neutral Pricing

Suppose we have a (European-style) derivative asset whose value at expiry (t=T) is given by a random variable X. The problem is to determine the market price Vt​ of this asset at times t<T. The absence of arbitrage in the market implies the following general risk-neutral pricing formula:Vt​=ertE[e−rTX∣Ft​].(1.2)The critical feature here is that the expectation is not calculated under the original probability measure Po but with respect to the the risk-neutral probability measure, which is characterized by the property that the discounted stock price,e−rtSt​,is a martingale. We will use P for that risk-neutral probability. It will be the underlying probability measure throughout; we will have virtually no need for the original Po.

The hypotheses on which the formula (1.2) is based are as follows.

•

The description of St​ and Bt​ is appropriate, and the values of α, r, and σ are known.

•

There are no transaction costs associated with buying and selling shares of stock or bond. Stock and bond may be held in any amounts (not limited to integral multiples or positive amounts) and can be traded continuously.

•

The stock pays no dividends.

•

For any time t≤T knowledge of the stock price history {Su​:u≤t} constitutes complete knowledge of the state of the market at time t. (I.e. there are no stochastic components of the model other than St​. The values of all market variables at time t are prescribed by knowledge of the stock price history.) The σ-algebra Ft​ is determined (or ”generated”) by this information.

•

X is FT​ measurable and E[X2]<∞. (Remember, this is with respect to the risk-neutral probability P.)

•

There are no arbitrage opportunities in the market. (Mathematically, this follows from the existence of the risk-neutral probability measure.)

An outline of how this leads to (1.2) is as follows. The effect of switching to the risk-neutral probability P is that the original Wto​ is no longer a Brownian motion. InsteadWt​=Wto​+(σα−r​)t(1.3)is a Brownian motion with respect to P. The equation for the stock price process can be reformulated asdSt​=rSt​dt+σSt​dWt​.(1.4)The solution can be written explicitly:St​=S0​e(r−σ2/2)t+σWt​.

Suppose that htB​ and htS​ comprise a self-financing portfolio with value process Vt​,Vt​dVt​​=htB​Bt​+htS​St​=htB​dBt​+htS​dSt​,​and which replicates X at time T:VT​=X.(This is always possible in the Black-Scholes model provided E[X2]<∞, by the completeness property and the martingale representation theorem.) Then it turns out that the discounted asset price Mt​=Vt​/Bt​ is also a Q-martingale. This is because its stochastic differential works out to bedMt​=σhtS​Bt​St​​dWt​,with no dt term. By the absence of arbitrage, Vt​ must agree with the market value at time t of the contingent claim. The risk neutral formula (1.2) is just the statement of this martingale property:Mt​=E[MT​∣Ft​], which we can rewrite as Vt​=Bt​E[X/Bt​∣Ft​].

When the value at expiry is a function of the stock price at expiry,X=ϕ(ST​),the market price will be given by a function v(s,t) of the current time and current stock price,Vt​=v(St​,t).This v(s,t) is called the pricing function for the contingent claim. The formula (1.2) reduces to a partial differential equation for v. We can see this if we use Itô’s formula to derive the stochastic differential of Vt​/Bt​=B0−1​e−rtv(St​,t): we obtaind[Vt​/Bt​]=Bt−1​([vt​(St​,t)+rsvs​(St​,t)+21​s2σ2vss​(St​,t)−rv(St​,t)]dt+vs​(St​,t)dWt​).Since Mt​=Vt​/Bt​ must be a Q-martingale, the coefficient of the dt term must be 0. Thus we find that v(s,t) satisfies the Black-Scholes Partial Differential Equation:21​s2σ2vss​+rsvs​−rv+vt​=0,for t<T,0<s(1.5)with the terminal condition v(s,T)=ϕ(s). This equation is equivalent to the martingale property of v(St​,t)/Bt​, and thus constitutes another expression of the risk-neutral formulation. Given ϕ(s) we want to solve the PDE (1.5) to find the pricing function v(s,t). The following figure illustrates the physical organization of this task.

The principle problem is to find the pricing function v. For the standard European options discussed above, this becomes the problem of solving the Black-Scholes PDE (1.5) with the given ϕ(s) as the terminal data. For some terminal value functions ϕ(s) explicit formulas for the solutions can be written down. A simple one is for a forward contract: ϕ(s)=s−K. In that case it is easy to check thatv(s,t)=s−Ke−r(T−t).The most famous explicit solution corresponds to a call option: ϕ(s)=(s−K)+. For this we get the Black-Scholes formula:vCall;K,T(s,t)N(y)d(1)d(2)​=sN(d(1))−Ke−r(T−t)N(d(2)), where=∫−∞y​2π​1​e−u2/2du,=σT−t​ln(s/K)+(r+21​σ2)(T−t)​,=d(1)(s,t)−σT−t​.​

We will use B to denote the differential operatorBv=21​σ2s2vss​+rsvs​−rv,so that the Black-Scholes equation (1.5) is described concisely asBv(s,t)+∂t​v(s,t)=0.(2.1)We are interested in solving this for 0<s, 0≤t≤T, with a prescribed terminal value functionv(s,T)=ϕ(s).(2.2)

In this chapter we present some basic theory describing this problem. We want to explain what kind of ϕ(s) can be considered; how we should understand (2.2) if ϕ(s) is discontinuous; whether there will always be a solution; and whether there can be more than one solution for the same ϕ(s). We will show that (2.1) is equivalent to the classical heat equation. The questions we just raised have all been answered for the heat equation, so we can simply translate results from the literature on the heat equation into the Black-Scholes context to obtain the answers to our questions. We will see in particular that there is an integral formula for the solution v in terms of ϕ(s). We will end the chapter with a collection of explicit solutions and simple transformations for constructing new solutions from old ones.

Introduction to Partial Differential Equations

To begin we want to place the Black-Scholes equation in the standard taxonomy of partial differential equations. The Black-Scholes PDE is a second order, linear, homogeneous equation. It is second order because the highest partial derivative involved is of second order. It is linear because the partial derivatives vs​, vss​, vt​ occur simply multiplied by known functions of the independent variables (s and t) and then added.

In general a second order linear PDE for a function u(x,t) takes the formauxx​+buxt​+cutt​+dux​+eut​+fu+g=0.(2.3)The coefficients are (prescribed) functions of the independent variables: a=a(x,t),…,g=g(x,t). When g=0 the equation is homogeneous. The problem is to find the function(s) u(x,t) which solve (2.3) for (x,t) in some region, usually in conjunction with some other “boundary conditions,” i.e. properties or values of the function which are specified on the boundary of the region. For (2.1) the region we are interested is the vertical strip0≤t≤T,0<sand the boundary condition is the requirement that v(s,T)=ϕ(s) for all s>0. There is no boundary condition specified for s=0 (or t=0); later in this chapter we will see why this is so.

Assuming that a, b, and c are not all zero (else the equation would not be second order), equations of the form (2.3) are usually categorized as one of three types: hyperbolic, parabolic, or elliptic. The best known examples of each type are the following.

•

Wave Equation (hyperbolic): uxx​−utt​=0.

•

Heat Equation (parabolic): uxx​−ut​=0.

•

Laplace Equation (elliptic): uxx​+uyy​=0.

Each of the three basic PDEs above has been thoroughly studied. Other equations of the same type (hyperbolic, parabolic, or elliptic) typically share many of the same properties as the appropriate one of these examples. The Black-Scholes equation is parabolic. In fact it is fully equivalent to the heat equation by means of a change of variables which we will work out in the next section. This is very convenient for us, because every question we might ask about the Black-Scholes equation can be translated into an analogous question about the heat equation. We can then turn to the extensive literature concerning the heat equation (or parabolic PDEs in general) to find the answer.

Conversion of Black-Scholes to the Heat Equation

We are going to develop a change of variables which converts solutions of the Black-Scholes equation (2.1) into solutions of the classical heat equation. We will work this out through a sequence of steps.

Step 1.

First we observe that in terms of y=log(s) the terms s∂s∂​ and s2∂s2∂2​ convert to constant multiples of ∂y∂​ and ∂y2∂2​. To be specific supposev(s,t)=f(y,t)=f(log(s),t)for some function f(y,t). Then we find from the chain rule thatsvs​(s,t)s2vss​(s,t)​=s⋅s1​fy​(log(s),t)=fy​(y,t),=s2[−s21​fy​(log(s),t)+s21​fyy​(log(s),t)]=fyy​(y,t)−fy​(y,t).​The time derivative is unchanged: vt​(s,t)=∂t​[f(log(s),t)]=ft​(y,t). If we make these substitutions in (2.1), we find that21​σ2s2vss​+rsvs​−rv+vt​=21​σ2fyy​+(r−21​σ2)fy​−rf+ft​,where the left side is evaluated at (s,t) and the right side is evaluated at the corresponding value of (y,t). So in terms of the new variable y=log(s) we find that v(s,t)=f(y,t) solves the Black-Scholes equation (2.1) if and only if f solves the equation21​σ2fyy​+(r−21​σ2)fy​+ft​−rf=0.(2.4)This gives us an equation with constant coefficients, as opposed to the variable coefficients of (2.1). Also observe that 0<s<∞ corresponds to −∞<y<∞.

Step 2.

We want to make additional variable changes to convert (2.4) into the heat equation. The next step is to eliminate the first order derivative fy​. This can be accomplished by a change of dependent variable:f(y,t)=ec1​yg(y,t),for a carefully chosen constant c1​. If we substitute this expression for f into (2.4) we obtainec1​y[21​σ2gyy​+(c1​σ2+r−21​σ2)gy​+gt​+(c1​−1)(r+c1​21​σ2)g]=0.Making the choicec1​=21​−σ2r​eliminates the gy​ term, so that equation (2.4) for f is equivalent to the following equation for g:21​σ2gyy​+gt​+(c1​−1)(r+c1​21​σ2)g=0.(2.5)

Step 3.

We next eliminate the undifferentiated term g by another change of dependent variable:g(y,t)=ec2​th(y,t).This makes (2.5) equivalent toec2​t[21​σ2hyy​+ht​+c2​h+(c1​−1)(r+c1​21​σ2)h]=0.We make the specific choicec2​=−(c1​−1)(r+c1​21​σ2)=8σ2(σ2+2r)2​.This makes (2.5) equivalent to21​σ2hyy​+ht​=0.(2.6)

Step 4.

Now we make one last change of variables to scale out the 21​σ2 and reverse the sign on the time derivative. With x=2​y/σ, τ=T−t andh(y,t)=e−c2​Tu(x,τ)=e−c2​Tu(2​y/σ,T−t)we find that (2.6) is equivalent to the heat equation:uxx​(x,τ)−uτ​(x,τ)=0.(2.7)

Now put all the steps together to obtain the conversion formula.v(s,t)​=f(y,t)=ec1​yg(y,t)=ec1​y+c2​th(y,t)=ec1​y+c2​te−c2​Tu(x,τ)=e(c1​σ/2​)x−c2​τu(x,τ).​Note that the role of e−c2​T in Step 4 is simply to get all the t occurring in the combination T−t=τ. This τ is the time variable we will use for the heat equation. It is different from the t in the Black-Scholes equation.

To make this change of variables convenient to refer to, define the parameters μ=c1​σ/2​ and ν=c2​. (Don’t confuse the Greek ν (“nu”) with the Latin v.) After simplifying the expressions for μ and ν, we havev(s,t)=eμx−ντu(x,τ),where(2.8)stμν​=eσx/2​,=T−τ,=2​1​(2σ​−σr​),=r+μ2.​

We will refer to v, s and t as financial variables and u, x, and τ as the corresponding heat variables. The above formulas establish a one-to-one conversion between functions v(s,t):(0,∞)×(−∞,T]→R and functions u(x,τ):(−∞,∞)×[0,∞)→R with the property thatBv(s,t)+∂t​v(s,t)=0 if and only if ∂x2​u(x,τ)−∂τ​u(x,τ)=0.

For the heat equation we usually start with values of u for τ=0 prescribed by some initial value function,u(x,0)=ψ(x),and solve for u as τ moves forward in time. For the Black-Scholes equation we start with values given at t=T by the terminal value function, v(s,T)=ϕ(s), and solve for v as t moves backwards in time. Observe that ψ(x) and ϕ(s) are connected by our change of variables:ϕ(s)=v(s,T)=eμxu(x,0)=eμxψ(x).

The Heat Equation: Existence and Uniqueness

We next summarize a number of important properties of the heat equationuxx​(x,τ)−uτ​(x,τ)=0;−∞<x<∞, τ≥0.

We will translate these into financial variables to obtain analogous properties of the Black-Scholes equation. (A good first reference on PDEs in general is F. John ’s PDE book. For a more extensive treatment of the heat equation specifically, see D. V. Widder’s The Heat Equation.)

First observe that if we know two solutions u(1) and u(2) of (2.7), then any linear combination of them will also be a solution. To see this consideru(x,τ)=c1​u(1)(x,τ)+c2​u(2)(x,τ),where c1​ and c2​ are any constants. Thenuxx​−uτ​​=(c1​uxx(1)​+c2​uxx(2)​)−(c1​uτ(1)​+c2​uτ(2)​)=c1​(uxx(1)​−uτ(1)​)+c2​(uxx(2)​−uτ(2)​)=0.​This property of combining solutions is called the principle of superposition.

There are many solutions to the heat equation. As we said above, we will usually have an initial function ψ(x) which prescribes initial data for the solution u we want. In other words, we require the solution to match ψ at τ=0:u(x,0)=ψ(x) for all x∈R.(2.9)

When we say u(x,τ) is a solution of (2.7) that obviously means that the partial derivatives uxx​ and uτ​ exist, as well as the fact that they are equal. The functions ψ(x) which are of interest to us for option pricing purposes are generally not differentiable for every x. So we can not insist that u(x,0)=ψ(x) be differentiable. In other words we can only expect that (2.7) holds for τ>0, not for τ=0. But we do want the values of u(x,0)=ψ(x) to be associated with the values of u(x,τ) for τ>0. Thus what we will mean by saying that u(x,τ) is a solution of the initial value problem (2.7) and (2.9) is that

•

u(x,τ) is continuous in x∈R and τ≥0,

•

u(x,0)=ψ(x) for all x∈R,

•

u(x,τ) is twice continuously differentiable in x∈R and once differentiable in τ for τ>0,

•

u(x,τ) satisfies (2.7) for all x∈R and τ>0.

Occasionally we need to consider ψ(x) which is discontinuous at a finite number of x-values: x1​, x2​, …. In that case we need to exclude (x,τ)=(xi​,0) from the first two bullets.

The heat equation is intimately connected to Brownian motion. We can exploit that to find a formula for u(x,τ) in terms of ψ(x). To see the connection, consider Mt​=u(2​Wt​,T−t) and apply Itô’s formula to see thatdMt​​=2​ux​dWt​+(21​⋅2uxx​−uτ​)dt=2​ux​dWt​,​by virtue of the heat equation. So (under some integrability assumptions on ux​) Mt​ will be a martingale. Using that we find thatu(2​Wt​,T−t)​=Mt​=E[MT​∣Ft​]=E[u(2​WT​,0)∣Ft​]=E[ψ(2​WT​)∣Ft​].​(2.11)

Conditioned on 2​Wt​=x, 2​WT​ is a normal random variable with mean x and variance 2(T−t). So, with τ=T−t>0 we can continue to work out the above asu(x,τ)​=∫−∞∞​ψ(y)2π⋅2(T−t)​1​e−(y−x)2/(2⋅2(T−t))dy=∫−∞∞​4πτ​1​e−(y−x)2/(4τ)ψ(y)dy=∫−∞∞​k(x,τ;y)ψ(y)dy.​(2.12)

The functionk(x,τ;y)=4πτ​1​e−(y−x)2/(4τ)occurring here is called the fundamental solution of the heat equation, or the heat kernel. (It’s also the transition density for 2​Wt​.) You can check that for a fixed y, k(x,τ;y) does solve the heat equation for τ>0. According to the principle of superposition, it follows that for any choice of values yj​ and constants cj​=ψ(yj​) the sumj=1∑N​ψ(yj​)k(x,τ;yj​)will also be a solution. We can view (2.12) as a limiting version of this construction. The reason (2.12) produces a solution with u(x,0)=ψ(x) is that as τ→0 the graph of y↦k(x,τ;y) “bunches up” at y=x, so that when τ is small the integral only uses values of ψ(y) for y very close to x.

The formula (2.12) is called a convolution because it is of the form ∫f(x−y)ψ(y)dy. The formula is very nice in that it tells us how to find the solution u for any given ψ. But it is not the whole story. There are two important issues. One is that for some functions ψ(x) the integral might fail to exist, particularly if ψ(x) grows too fast as x→±∞. Secondly, it turns out that even for the nicest ψ(x), there are always other solutions of the heat equation with u(x,0)=ψ(x); (2.12) gives only one of many possible solutions! For instance, if ψ(x)=0 then (2.12) produces u(x,τ)=0, but there are other solutions with u(x,0)=0 which have u(x,τ)=0 for τ>0. So how do we know if the solution produced by (2.12) is the one we want, or if we should be looking for one of the others? What sets the solution from (2.12) apart from the others? The following theorem provides an answer to both of these issues.

Theorem 14.1. Suppose ψ(x) is a continuous function of x∈R with the property that1+∣x∣log(1+∣ψ(x)∣)​ is a bounded function.(2.13)Then the integral in (2.12) does exist for all x and τ>0, the resulting function u(x,τ) solves the heat equation for τ>0 and is a continuous function of x∈R and τ≥0 with u(x,0)=ψ(x). Moreover u is the only such solution with the property that for each T<∞,1+∣x∣log(1+∣u(x,τ)∣)​ is a bounded function of x∈R, 0≤τ≤T.(2.14)

We want to digest what this theorem says. Suppose K is a bound on the expression (2.14). That implies that for all 0≤τ≤T and all x,∣u(x,τ)∣≤eKeK∣x∣.On the other hand if there are positive constants k1​ and k2​ so that∣u(x,τ)∣≤k1​ek2​∣x∣,(2.15)then1+∣u(x,τ)∣​≤(k1​+1)ek2​∣x∣=elog(1+k1​)+k2​∣x∣≤eK(1+∣x∣),​where K=max(log(1+k1​),k2​). Thus (2.14) is just a way of saying that (given T) there exist constants k1​ and k2​ for which (2.15) holds. We can describe this by saying that u grows at most exponentially as ∣x∣→±∞. What the theorem tells us is that if ψ(x) grows at most exponentially, then the integral formula (2.12) does indeed produce a solution with initial data ψ, and the solution it produces is the only solution which grows at most exponentially. All the other solutions fail to satisfy the exponential growth condition (2.14).

When ψ(x) is discontinuous at a finite number of points the assertions of the theorem remain true if we are careful about the sense in which u(x,0)=ψ(x). Now u will be continuous at all (x,τ) with τ>0 and at those (x,0) for which ψ is continuous at x. And we can only say that u(x,0)=ψ(x) at the continuity points of ψ(x). With these adjustments, the theorem above remains true.

The Heat Equation on a Strip

We also need to understand the heat equation when x is limited to an interval. Suppose we want to limit x to an interval xL≤x≤xH. Then we would want to solve the heat equation on the “strip”uxx​−uτ​=0 for xL≤x≤xH,0<τ,with prescribed initial valuesu(x,0)=ψ(x) for xL≤x≤xH.This by itself is not enough information to determine the solution u(x,τ). In addition we need to know the values of u(xL,τ) and u(xH,τ) along the bottom and top of the strip. If we are given functions uL(τ) and uH(τ) then, in addition to the heat equation and initial values, we also want to ask that the solution satisfy the boundary conditionsu(xL,τ)=uL(τ) and u(xH,τ)=uH(τ),τ>0.(2.16)If ψ(x), uL(τ) and uH(τ) are continuous with agreement at the corners (ψ(xL)=uL(0) and ψ(xH)=uH(0)) then there will be a unique function u(x,τ) which is continuous in the (closed) strip solving the heat equation and the prescribed initial and boundary conditions. Since x is bounded, there are no growth conditions as ∣x∣→∞ to worry about; the boundary conditions (2.16) have essentially taken over that role. If there are a finite number of points of discontinuity for uL, uH, and ψ, or mismatch at the corners (ψ(xL)=uL(0) or ψ(xH)=uH(0)) then u will not be continuous at those discontinuity points and will fail to satisfy the initial or boundary conditions at those particular points. However the existence and uniqueness of the solution still hold.

A formula like (2.12) which gives the solution u explicitly in terms of ψ, uL, and uH is possible, using either Fourier series (the method of “separation of variables”) or theta-functions (see [32]). We will not write it down, because it would take us too far afield and we will not need it for any purpose below.

The Heat Equation on a Semi-Strip

The heat equation can also be considered on a semi-infinite strip like−∞<x≤xH,0<τ.In that case a boundary condition is needed at x=xH:u(xH,τ)=uH(τ) for all τ>0,and a growth condition (2.13) and (2.14) as x→−∞. (Or we could use the strip with xL≤x with a boundary condition at x=xL and a growth condition for x→+∞.) The theory of this kind of problem is analogous to that described above.

Example. Suppose we want to solve the above problem with uH(τ)=1 and ψ(x)=0. We can tease a formula for the solution out of (2.12) by extending the definition of ψ(x) to x>xH:ψ(x)={20​if x>xH,if x≤xH.​Let u(x,τ) be the solution produced by (2.12).u(x,τ)=∫xH∞​2k(x,τ;y)dy=2N(2τ​x−xH​).It solves the heat equation for all x∈R, τ>0. So for x<xH we have u(x,0)=ψ(x)=0. For x=xH and τ>0 we find thatu(xH,τ)=∫k(xH,τ;y)ψ(y)dy=2∫xH∞​4πτ​1​e−(y−xH)2/(4τ)dy=1.Thus this is the solution we sought. (There is a mismatch at the corner, so strictly speaking neither the boundary or initial conditions hold at x=xH, τ=0.)

The solution of this example has a useful interpretation for Brownian motion. Pick a value b, take xH=2​b and let u(x,τ) be the solution above. We know thatMt​=u(2​Wt​,T−t)is a martingale. Let Tb be the first time the Brownian motion Wt​ reaches the value b. Then Mt∧Tb​ is also a martingale, so we can writeu(0,T)​=M0​=E[MT∧Tb​]=E[u(2​b,T−Tb);Tb≤T]+E[u(2​WT​,0);T<Tb]=E[1;Tb≤T]+E[0;T<Tb]=P(Tb≤T).​Thus u(0,T) provides a formula for the distribution function of the first passage time Tb of Brownian motion:P(Tb≤T)=u(0,T)=2N(2T​−2​b​)=2N(−b/T​).By differentiating with respect to T>0 we calculate the density of Tb to be 2π​b​t−3/2e−b2/(2t), for t>0.

The Black-Scholes Equation: Existence and Uniqueness

We can now use our change of variables (2.8) to translate the results for the heat equation into analogous results for the Black-Scholes equation. Especially important is what the growth condition (2.14), or equivalently (2.15), becomes in terms of financial variables. Because s=eσx/2​, we see that x∈R corresponds to 0<s and we havee∣x∣={s2​/σs−2​/σ​for s≥1,for 0<s<1​=max(s,1/s)2​/σ.Thus (2.15) means that∣v(s,t)∣​≤s2​μ/σe−ν(T−t)k1​max(s,1/s)k2​2​/σ=e−ν(T−t)k1​{sσ2​​(μ+k2​)(1/s)σ2​​(k2​−μ)​for s≥1,for 0<s<1.​​It follows that (2.15) in heat variables (for 0≤τ≤T) is equivalent to saying that in financial variables there exist constants mi​ so that∣v(s,t)∣≤{m1​sm2​m1​(1/s)m2​​when s≥1,when 0<s<1​(2.17)for 0≤t≤T. We describe this by saying that v grows at most polynomially in s as s→∞, and in 1/s as s→0. Here is what our theorem about the heat equation says when translated to the Black-Scholes equation.

Theorem 14.2. Suppose that ϕ(s) is a continuous function defined for s>0 which grows at most polynomially in s as s→∞ and in 1/s as s→0. Then there is a unique function v(s,t) defined and continuous for 0<s and 0≤t≤T which solves the Black-Scholes equation (1.5) for 0<s and t<T, satisfies v(s,T)=ϕ(s), and which grows at most polynomially in s as s→∞ and in 1/s as s→0. This solution is given by the integral formulav(s,t)=e−r(T−t)∫0∞​q(s,t;z,T)ϕ(z)dz,(2.18)whereq(s,t;z,T)g(τ,x)​=g(T−t,sz​)s1​,=σ2πτ​1​e−μ2(T−t)x−(1+σ2​μ​+2τσ21​log(x)),​μ and ν being the parameters defined in (2.8).

The integral formula is simply the result of takingψ(x)=u(x,0)=e−μxv(eσx/2​,T)=e−μxϕ(eσx/2​),using it in (2.12), and then changing back to financial variables (y=2​log(z)/σ, ψ(y)=e−μyϕ(z)).v(s,t)​=e−ν(T−t)+μx∫−∞∞​k(x,τ;y)ψ(y)dy=e−ν(T−t)∫−∞∞​k(x,τ;y)eμxe−μyϕ(z)dy=e−r(T−t)∫0∞​e−μ2(T−t)k(x,τ;y)eμ(x−y)ϕ(z)σ2​​z1​dz=e−r(T−t)∫0∞​q(s,t;z,T)ϕ(z)dz.​

We obtain the formula (2.19) for q(s,t;z,T) by substituting variables and simplifying the expressionq(s,t;z,T)=e−μ2(T−t)σ2​​eμ(x−y)k(x,τ;y)z1​.

We could arrive at this formula directly from the risk-neutral expressionv(s,t)​=e−r(T−t)E[ϕ(ST​)∣St​=s]=e−r(T−t)∫0∞​q(s,t;z,T)ϕ(z)dz,​where q is the transition density for the stock price process, under the risk neutral probability.

The integral formula (2.18) is only of theoretical interest. Although it could be implemented numerically, it would probably be easier to convert ϕ(s) to ψ(x); evaluate (2.12), and then convert back to financial variables. What is significant about the theorem is that, unlike the heat equation on a semi-strip, the Black-Scholes equation does not require boundary values for v(0,t) to be specified in order to determine a unique solution. We don’t really consider s=0 to even be a legitimate value of the variable s; it corresponds to x=−∞ in heat variables. Given ϕ(s), all that we require about v(s,t) for s≈0 is that v(s,t) is bounded by some power of 1/s as s↓0. This does not mean that lims↓0​v(s,t) does not exist or is undetermined. It only means that we don’t need values of v(0,t) to be prescribed in order to determine v. In fact, as we will see in Section 3.3, if ϕ(0)=lims↓0​ϕ(s) exists then lims↓0​v(s,t)=e−r(T−t)ϕ(0).

Polynomial Growth and Risk-Neutral Pricing

The solutions v(s,t) of (2.1) and (2.2) that we are interested in are those which come from the risk neutral pricing formulav(St​,t)=E[e−r(T−t)ϕ(ST​)∣Ft​].(2.20)We want to be sure that these are the solutions to which the above theorem applies, in other words that they do satisfy the polynomial growth conditions of the theorem. What makes this true is that all the terminal value functions ϕ(s) that we are interested in satisfy a linear bound:∣ϕ(s)∣≤Cs+C, for some nonnegative constant C and all s>0.(2.21)

Consider some of our typical choices for ϕ(s).

•

For a forward, ϕ(s)=s−K, so ∣ϕ(s)∣≤s+K. So (2.21) holds with C=K.

•

For a call or put, ϕ(s)=(s−K)±, so again ∣ϕ(s)∣≤s+K.

•

Even for something more complicated, like a chooser (T<Ti​): ϕ(s)=max(vCall;K1​,T1​(s,T),vPut;K2​,T2​(s,T)),because of the bounds 0≤vCall;K1​,T1​(s,T)=sN(d1​)−K1​e−r(T1​−T)N(d2​)≤s,and 0≤vPut;K2​,T2​(s,T)=−s[1−N(d1​)]+K2​e−r(T2​−T)[1−N(d2​)]≤K2​,we have ∣ϕ(s)∣≤s+K2​. Thus (2.21) holds.

If we use the linear bound (2.21) in the risk-neutral formula, we obtain∣v(St​,t)∣​≤e−r(T−t)EQ[∣ϕ(ST​)∣∣Ft​]≤e−r(T−t)EQ[CST​+C∣Ft​]=CSt​+e−r(T−t)C.​Therefore for all t<T, v satisfies the same linear bound as ϕ:∣v(s,t)∣≤Cs+C.This clearly satisfies the polynomial growth condition both as s→∞ and s→0. Thus the pricing functions v produced by the risk-neutral formula using ϕ(s) satisfying the linear growth condition (2.21) do correspond to solutions of the Black-Scholes equation described by our theorem above.

Solution Transformations

Suppose u(x,τ) solves the heat equation. It is easy to check that bothu~(x,τ)=u(x+c,τ)andu~(x,τ)=u(−x,τ)also solve the heat equation. If we start with a solution v(s,t) of the Black-Scholes equation, convert it to a solution of the heat equation using (2.8), apply one of the above, and then convert back to financial variables, we discover that the following transformations convert any solution v of the Black-Scholes equation to a new solution v~:v~(s,t)v~(s,t)​=v(cs,t)any constant c>0,(2.22)=sκv(s−1,t)where κ=1−σ22r​=2​σμ.(2.23)​These are verified by direct calculation.

The Basic Solutions v(0)-v(5)
